title: Timing and datasheets
summary: Memories have timing rules just like flip-flops — setup, hold, clock-to-output, cycle time — and stand-alone SRAMs have their own asynchronous cycles. This topic teaches you to read a memory datasheet, compute the clock limit of a path through a memory, and verify a memory with a behavioural model and a self-checking testbench.
objectives: Explain setup, hold, clock-to-output and cycle time of a memory macro.
Read a memory datasheet and compute the maximum clock frequency of a path.
Describe asynchronous SRAM read and write cycles.
Write a behavioural memory model with timing checks and a self-checking testbench.

blocks.md: An SRAM macro behaves like a big register bank with timing rules at its pins:

steps.title: Setup time tSU
steps.md: Address, enables and data must be stable **before** the rising edge.

steps.title: Hold time tH
steps.md: …and stay stable for a short time **after** it.

steps.title: Clock-to-output tCQ
steps.md: Read data becomes valid tCQ after the edge — the macro's access time.

steps.title: Cycle time tCYC
steps.md: The minimum clock period: one access per tCYC.

blocks.title: Two timing paths through every memory
blocks.md: **Into** the memory: logic delay + tSU must fit in the clock period. **Out of** the memory: tCQ + logic delay + the setup of the next flip-flop must fit. The output path is usually the critical one — which is why output registers (latency 2) exist.
A memory compiler produces a datasheet for every generated instance. A typical excerpt (illustrative numbers for one instance and corner):

**Worked example.** The read data goes through 0.9 ns of logic into a flip-flop with 0.1 ns setup:

> period ≥ tCQ + logic + tSU(FF) = 0.6 + 0.9 + 0.1 = **1.6 ns** → at most 625 MHz.

With an output register (latency 2) the logic moves to the next stage: period ≥ max(tCYC, tCQ + tSU(FF)) = 1.0 ns → 1 GHz.

blocks.title: Corners
blocks.md: Values are given per **corner**: slow process, low voltage, high temperature for the worst case; fast corners for hold checks. Timing analysis uses all of them.
Stand-alone SRAM chips (and some old designs) have **no clock**. Control signals are active-low: /CE (chip enable), /OE (output enable), /WE (write enable).

steps.title: Read cycle
steps.md: Data appears tAA after the address is stable — once /CE and /OE are low (tOE after /OE).

steps.title: Write cycle
steps.md: The cell is written while /WE is low for at least tWP; data must be valid tDW before /WE rises.

The testbench writes random data to random addresses, keeps a **reference model** (an associative array) and compares every read:

items.title: Why drive at the falling edge?
items.md: Inputs change half a period before the rising edge, so setup and hold are met with a large margin — the testbench checks function, the specify block checks timing.

items.title: Why an associative array?
items.md: It stores only the addresses that were written. `exists()` tells whether a read address has a known expected value — unwritten addresses are skipped.

items.title: What next?
items.md: Lab **M1** extends this testbench: byte enables, read-during-write checks, back-to-back accesses and coverage of all addresses.

questions.text: What does the setup time tSU of a memory macro require?
options: Inputs stable for tSU before the rising clock edge
Data valid tSU after the edge
A clock period of at least tSU
Inputs stable tSU after the edge

questions.text: tCQ = 0.8 ns, logic after the memory = 1.0 ns, flip-flop setup = 0.2 ns. Minimum clock period?
In an asynchronous SRAM read, what is tAA?
options: Time from a stable address to valid data

questions.text: What happens in sram_model when a setup or hold check fails?
options: The notifier toggles and q becomes X

questions.text: Why does the testbench use an associative array as reference model?
options: It only stores written addresses, and exists() tells which reads can be checked
It is faster than the DUT

questions.text: In the model, why is the read written as `q <= #(T_CQ) mem[a];`?
options: Because non-blocking assignments need a delay
